client: I've been feeling really stretched thin lately, like no matter how hard I try, I can't keep up with everything. My graduate program demands so much from me — the readings, the papers, the expectations — and then I have to go straight to my shift at the coffee shop and pretend everything's fine. I'm honestly not sure talking about it is going to change the fact that I have too much on my plate, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a really heavy load right now — juggling intense academic demands with work, all while keeping up a brave face, and that kind of sustained pressure can leave anyone feeling depleted. I hear your skepticism too, and I think it's actually pretty courageous to show up and try anyway, even when you're not sure it'll help. I'm curious — when you imagine "keeping up with everything," what does that actually look like to you, and whose definition of "enough" are you measuring yourself against?

client: Honestly, when I picture "keeping up," it means finishing every reading before seminar, turning in papers that are actually good — not just adequate — and still being present enough at work that my manager doesn't think I'm slacking. I guess the definition comes from... my advisor, my program, but also just from me, because I've always been someone who finishes what they start and doesn't complain about it. That question kind of stings a little, because I think I already know the answer is that the bar I've set is probably unrealistic, but admitting that feels like giving myself permission to fail.
therapist: That insight you just named — that admitting the bar is too high feels like permission to fail — is really worth sitting with, because it reveals a belief that's doing a lot of work beneath the surface: that lowering an impossible standard is the same as giving up, rather than being a reasonable response to reality. There's a difference between *finishing what you start* and *finishing everything perfectly while running on empty*, and it sounds like somewhere along the way those two things got fused together for you. What do you think it would actually mean about you as a person if you turned in a paper that was "good" rather than exceptional — what's the fear underneath that?

client: I think the fear is that if I turn in something just "good," my advisor will see through me and realize I don't actually belong in the program. Like, the exceptional work is the only thing standing between me and being found out as someone who got in by mistake. It's embarrassing to say out loud, but I think I've been operating on the assumption that I have to keep proving I deserve to be there, every single time.
therapist: What you just described has a name — it's called impostor syndrome — and the fact that it feels embarrassing to say out loud actually speaks to how convincing that inner voice has been, not to any truth about your belonging. It's worth gently challenging the evidence here: you were admitted to a competitive graduate program, you're managing coursework *and* a job, and your advisor has presumably seen your work and not asked you to leave. What would you say to a close friend in your exact situation who told you they were secretly terrified they didn't belong — would the evidence look the same to you from the outside?

client: I know what I'd tell a friend — I'd say the evidence clearly shows they belong, that getting in was proof enough, and that one imperfect paper doesn't erase everything they've worked for. But when I try to apply that same logic to myself, it just... doesn't land the same way, it feels like I'm making excuses for myself rather than being rational. I think part of me believes I'm a special case, like the rules of reasonable thinking apply to everyone else but my situation is somehow different.
therapist: What you just described — "I'm the exception to rational thinking" — is actually one of the most common and sneaky features of impostor syndrome, and it's worth naming that this belief *itself* is the distortion, not evidence that you're a special case. The fact that the compassionate logic lands so easily for a friend but bounces off when you turn it toward yourself suggests this isn't really about evidence at all — it's about a different standard you've learned to hold yourself to, one that may have served you at some point but is now costing you a lot. I'm wondering — can you think of where that double standard might have come from, maybe earlier in your life when proving yourself felt especially necessary?

client: I think it probably goes back to being the first person in my family to go to college — there was this unspoken pressure to justify the sacrifices my parents made, and "good enough" was never really a phrase that existed in that context. Every achievement felt less like something to celebrate and more like evidence I hadn't failed yet, if that makes sense. I can see the connection you're drawing, but I'm not sure digging into where it came from actually helps me get through next week's seminar and Thursday's shift without falling apart.
therapist: What you just shared about your family context is really meaningful, and you're right to flag the practical urgency — understanding the roots matters, but so does getting through Thursday in one piece. What the connection does offer you *right now* is this: that relentless inner voice demanding you prove yourself isn't a accurate read of your current reality, it's an old survival strategy that made sense then but is running on autopilot in a context where you've already made it. So as a small, concrete step — what would "good enough to survive this week" actually look like in practice, if you let yourself define it on your own terms rather than the ones you inherited?

client: I guess "good enough this week" would look like submitting the paper even if I haven't rewritten the introduction three times, and getting through my shifts without mentally rehearsing everything I should be doing instead. But honestly, just defining it that way makes me anxious, like I'm already setting myself up to underperform and then I'll have to live with that. I think the hard part is that even if I intellectually agree this is a reasonable approach, I don't trust that I won't spiral into guilt afterward when the paper isn't what I wanted it to be.
therapist: There's something really honest in what you just said — you can see the reasonable path, you can even name it clearly, but you don't yet trust yourself to feel okay walking it, and that gap between knowing and feeling is often where the real work lives. One thing worth noticing is that you're essentially predicting a spiral that hasn't happened yet and treating that prediction as fact, which means the anxiety is doing its job of keeping the old standard in place before you've even tried. What if we got specific — if you did submit that paper without the third rewrite and the guilt did show up afterward, what's one thing you could say to yourself in that moment that might be even a little more compassionate than what your default voice usually offers?

client: Maybe something like... "You did the best you could with the time and energy you actually had, not the time and energy you wished you had." But even as I say that, I notice I'm kind of cringing at it, like it sounds too soft, too much like letting myself off the hook. I wonder if I'd actually be able to access that thought in the moment when the guilt is loud, or if it would just feel hollow compared to how real the self-criticism feels.
therapist: That phrase you came up with is actually really good — and the cringe you feel toward it is worth paying attention to, because it tells you something important: self-compassion feels *dangerous* to you right now, not just soft, like it might lower your guard and let something bad happen. The self-criticism feels more "real" partly because it's been practiced for years and has a familiar weight to it, while the compassionate thought is new and untested — but that's a difference in *habit*, not in truth. What do you think the self-critical voice is actually protecting you from, in those moments after you submit something imperfect?

client: I think the self-critical voice is protecting me from being caught off guard — like if I beat everyone else to the criticism, it hurts less when it comes from the outside, from my advisor or my professors. There's almost a superstitious quality to it, like if I stay hard on myself, I'm less likely to get complacent and actually fail. But hearing you frame it as "protection" is strange, because I never thought of the self-criticism as something doing a job for me — I always just experienced it as the truth.
therapist: What you just landed on is genuinely significant — recognizing that the self-criticism is a *strategy* rather than the truth is one of those shifts that can slowly change everything, because you can question a strategy in a way you can't really question what feels like plain reality. That superstitious logic — "stay harsh and you'll stay safe" — made a lot of sense as a way to survive high-stakes situations where you felt like you couldn't afford to be blindsided, but it also means you've been living under a constant low-grade threat that never fully turns off. I'm curious: now that you can see it as something your mind *does* rather than something that's simply *true*, does that change anything about how you want to relate to it going forward?

client: It does change something, even if I can't fully feel it yet — there's a small part of me that feels less trapped by it, like maybe I have a little more say in whether I listen to it or not. But I'm also worried that understanding it intellectually in this room is very different from remembering any of this when I'm exhausted after a double shift and staring at a draft I hate at midnight. I guess I'm asking, how do I actually hold onto this when the conditions are the worst possible ones for clear thinking?
therapist: That small shift you're noticing — even if it's more intellectual than felt right now — is actually how this work starts, and it's worth trusting that a little. For the midnight-draft moments, the goal isn't to remember everything we talked about, it's to have one small anchor — and that phrase you created earlier, "the best you could with the time and energy you actually had," could live somewhere physical, a note on your laptop or your phone, so your exhausted self doesn't have to generate it from scratch. What would it look like to build even one tiny structure this week that makes it slightly easier to access a kinder voice when the conditions are working against you?

client: I could probably put something on a sticky note on my laptop, that's small enough that it doesn't feel ridiculous. But I'm a little skeptical that seeing a phrase I wrote down is going to cut through the noise when I'm genuinely spiraling — it might just feel like a hollow reminder that I was supposed to be kinder to myself and failed at that too. I think my worry is that even the tools for self-compassion become another thing I can do wrong.
therapist: That worry — that even self-compassion becomes a test you can fail — is such a clear window into how deep this pattern runs, and it actually makes a lot of sense given everything you've shared today. The sticky note isn't a performance you have to get right; it's just a small interruption, a half-second pause that gives you the tiniest opening to choose something different, and even if it only works once out of five spirals, that's still one moment of less suffering than before. I'm wondering — what would it mean to you if the goal of the sticky note wasn't to "fix" the spiral, but just to remind you that a kinder voice exists at all?
